planting.note: Set divisions into moist, humus-rich cracks among limestone boulders or tufa in deep shade; this fern needs constant moisture and a pH near neutral to slightly alkaline and will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Hairy maidenhair fern is known from only a couple of central Texas Hill Country counties, where it roots in perpetually damp limestone crevices along spring-fed river banks, far more restricted in range than its common cousin southern maidenhair. Its fronds are finer and noticeably fuzzy compared to Adiantum capillus-veneris, giving it a delicate, lacy texture that stands out in a shaded limestone garden. It carries no showy flowers, so its value is purely textural and as a conservation-minded specimen for collectors recreating Edwards Plateau seep habitat. Because it naturally grows wedged into wet rock rather than garden soil, it is considered difficult outside of consistently moist, well-drained, shaded crevice plantings.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions 6 to 12 inches apart in fall or spring; it adapts to a wide range of soils and tolerates both heat and light foot traffic once established.

directions: Edwards Plateau sedge forms dense, fine-textured evergreen clumps across Cross Timbers and Hill Country woodlands and clearings in central Texas and Oklahoma, fruiting in spring with inconspicuous flower spikes that offer little pollinator draw but valuable cover for small insects. It is unusually tolerant for a Carex, growing equally well in open sun or the dappled shade of oak-juniper woodland edges, and it shrugs off both summer heat and drought once rooted. Its tough, grass-like clumps make it a popular low-maintenance substitute for turf in shaded or part-shade areas where traditional lawn grasses struggle. Gardeners in the Hill Country prize it for staying green through winter and resisting the dry-shade die-back common to other groundcovers.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into thin soil pockets or crevices on limestone or other calcareous rock in dry shade; this desert fern needs sharp drainage far more than rich soil and resents standing moisture.

directions: Cochise scaly cloak fern grows wild on rocky canyon slopes and under boulder overhangs across the desert Southwest from Arizona and New Mexico into Trans-Pecos Texas, usually rooted in calcareous rock crevices rather than open soil. Its narrow fronds are covered in star-shaped scales that give the foliage a silvery, textured look and allow the plant to curl and desiccate during drought, then rehydrate and green up again after rain. It bears no flowers and offers no significant pollinator value, but it is prized by rock-garden and xeriscape growers for filling shaded nooks where few other ferns can survive. Unlike moisture-loving maidenhairs, it genuinely wants a dry, shaded, well-drained rock crevice and declines quickly in rich garden soil.

planting.note: Sow or transplant into rocky, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; established plants tolerate dry, lean ground typical of Edwards Plateau woodland understories.

directions: Drummond's wild petunia is a Texas Hill Country native that spends much of the growing season as an unassuming upright stem before opening trumpet-shaped purple flowers from leaf axils through summer and into late fall. Its blooms attract bees and long-tongued pollinators, and the foliage serves as a larval host plant for the Common Buckeye butterfly, giving it real wildlife value beyond ornament. Found mainly on the Edwards Plateau and locally north toward the Dallas area, it favors rocky, dry soils in the shade of oak-juniper woodland rather than open sun. Once established it needs very little supplemental water, making it a dependable, low-input choice for shaded native plantings.

planting.note: Direct sow or divide tubers in fall on rocky slopes or along canyon streambanks in partial shade; well-drained, gravelly soil is essential since the tuberous root rots in heavy, wet ground.

directions: Desert anemone emerges from a woody tuber on rocky canyon slopes and streambanks across the desert Southwest, from Arizona and New Mexico into West Texas and northern Mexico, opening white to pale pink flowers on slender stems in early to late spring. Its blooms draw small native bees and other early-season pollinators at a time when canyon shade plantings otherwise offer little nectar. The finely divided basal leaves die back by summer as the plant goes dormant to survive the dry season on reserves stored in its tuber. It performs best in gritty, fast-draining soil in the light shade of canyon walls or desert riparian woodland, where it gets moisture during winter and spring but dries out in summer heat.

planting.note: Plant divisions 9 to 15 inches apart in the loose, humus-rich duff found beneath Ashe juniper or oak canopy; this sedge is adapted to dry shade and declines in open, irrigated turf conditions.

directions: Cedar sedge is one of the defining groundcovers of Texas Hill Country oak-juniper woodlands, forming low, fine-textured clumps in the loose, fast-draining duff that accumulates under dense stands of Ashe juniper, from which its common name derives. It flowers and sets seed in the cool, moist conditions of early spring, with inconspicuous spikes that provide minor cover value rather than showy bloom or significant pollinator forage. Its particular talent is persisting in deep, dry shade where turfgrass and most other groundcovers fail, spreading slowly outward by short rhizomes to knit together bare ground beneath the canopy. It needs essentially no irrigation once established and is best used as a low-maintenance floor planting under native cedar or oak cover.
